Step back in time in Pioneer Square, Seattle’s original downtown. Cobblestone streets wind through historic buildings, creating a picturesque setting for charming boutiques. Find everything from handcrafted jewellery to bespoke home décor, all infused with the influence of the Pacific Northwest.

Stroll through Ballard Square, where indie boutiques showcase Seattle’s trendsetting style. Chic clothing, bold accessories and unique finds evoke an artistic vibe that reflects the city’s creative spirit.

Head back to Pike Place and Waterfront for souvenir shopping, where you can browse locally made crafts and gourmet treats that capture the essence of Seattle.
US.SEA.destinationPageIntro: Surrounded by mountains, water and parkland, Seattle is the largest city in the State of Washington and home to the iconic Space Needle landmark. Make sure to visit its bustling downtown area and explore its thriving arts and culture scene.
US.SEA.overviewText:
Nestled between evergreen mountains and the sparkling waters of the Pacific Northwest, Seattle is a unique city where nature, culture and innovation blend seamlessly. It’s no wonder they call it the Emerald City! It has an infectious energy and a creative spirit that’s as strong as its coffee.

From the iconic Space Needle to the bustling Pike Place Market, there’s always something exciting happening in Seattle. You’ll find charming boutiques, cosy cafés, quirky dining spots and cutting-edge landmarks around every corner. With so much to discover, your Seattle itinerary will practically plan itself.
US.SEA.eatingImageText:
Begin your culinary journey at Pike Place Market, where the aromas of fresh seafood, baked goods and roasted coffee beans fill the air. Watch the legendary fishmongers toss the day’s catch before indulging in a hearty fish stew called clam chowder. Or, try some buttery, melt-in-your-mouth oysters. This local favourite is served with a squeeze of lemon or a tangy mignonette sauce – a condiment made with minced shallots, cracked pepper and vinegar.

Seattle’s coffee culture is second to none, with indie coffee shops around every corner. Step into one of these cosy nooks for a perfectly brewed cup paired with a freshly baked pastry.

For something sweet, treat yourself to a slice or marionberry pie. This regional specialty is made with fresh, juicy marionberries, sugar, lemon and baked in a double-crust for a sweet and slightly tart flavour.

US.SFO.overviewTabHeading: Book your visit to San Francisco
US.SFO.businessClassSummary:
Fly to San Francisco in Business or First Class with Qatar Airways and indulge in ultimate luxury. From the moment you step into the airport to the moment you land, our world-renowned team are on hand to ensure that every part of your journey is tailored to your unique needs. 

Begin with effortless check-in before enjoying a peaceful break in one of our Business Class lounges. Here, you can use the private workstations to catch up on emails, or savour a cool beverage with a light snack. To freshen up, take an invigorating shower before your flight.  

Once on board our modern aircraft, our cabin crew show you to your spacious seat where you can stretch out thanks to the ergonomic design and extra legroom. Have a video call with family and friends or take part in a business meeting by connecting to the high-speed Wi-Fi (available on our A380, A350, B787 and select B777 aircraft).  

Then delight in a gourmet meal from our à la carte menu, freshly prepared by our award-winning chefs, followed by a film or TV show from our vast entertainment selection. When you need to rest, get some sleep on a lie-flat bed with soft linen, and let the ambient lighting synchronise your body to your destination’s time zone. Arrive feeling rejuvenated and ready to do business or spend time with loved ones.  

Book a flight to San Francisco in First or Business Class with Qatar Airways and travel in unmatched comfort.
US.SFO.touristAttractionsText:
Hop on an iconic cable car and hear the bells ring as you zip up and down the city’s famous hills. Step off at the top of Lombard Street, the world’s most crooked street. Walk your way down, and admire the manicured gardens and homes built along it.

Visit the stores and eateries on Fisherman’s Wharf then head to Pier 39, where the sea lions bark and bask in the sun. It’s incredible how many of them crowd around this lively pier.

A trip to Alcatraz Prison is not to be missed. The infamous island is spine-tingling as you browse the eerie cell blocks. There’s a magnificent view of San Francisco Bay from there too.

For something different, make your way to the Sutro Baths. The historic ruins of a once-grand bathhouse are set on the rugged coastline. It’s quite the marvel!
US.SFO.leisureActivitiesText:
Rent a bike and pedal across the Golden Gate Bridge. Soak in breathtaking views of the bay along the way and the impressive red structure. Coast into Sausalito, the quaint town on the other side of the bridge. This picturesque village is the perfect spot for a well-deserved ice cream.

For a glimpse of California’s giant redwoods, the Muir Woods National Monument is the place to be. Walk among these majestic trees that have earned their reputation as the tallest on earth.

Back in town, take a walking tour of Mission District to admire street art. Murals create vibrant alleyways, telling stories of culture, passion and history.

Spend an evening at the San Francisco Theater to catch a Broadway production or exclusive musicals. It makes for an entertaining activity for couples, families and even solo travellers.
US.SFO.businessClassTitle: Business Class flights to San Francisco
US.SFO.shoppingText:
Naturally, you should go to one of the largest downtown shopping areas in the USA, Union Square. Wander around this thriving hub of high-end retailers, flagship stores and chic boutiques.

For a more refined shopping experience, explore Hayes Valley. Browse through elegant clothing stores, trendy home décor shops and unique accessories – each offering carefully curated collections. It’s a must-visit for fashion enthusiasts to find something distinctive.

Immerse yourself in San Francisco’s artistic charm by exploring areas known for artsy, locally created treasures, such as Mission District and Haight-Ashbury. From handmade jewellery to art, boho clothes and vintage finds – it’s impossible to leave empty-handed.
US.SFO.touristAttractionsTabHeading: Things to do in San Francisco
US.SFO.destinationPageIntro: From cycling over the Golden Gate Bridge to its quirky shopping scene, explore San Francisco to discover an adventure like no other.
US.SFO.overviewText:
San Francisco has a vibe of its own, where the old mingles with the new, and the ocean meets the city. In addition to its innovative, tech-driven influence, each neighbourhood is bursting with quirky charm. One minute you’re savouring a pastry in a bohemian café, the next you’re drawn into an impromptu street performance. The hilly, winding streets are alive with art and culture.

The city offers a treasure trove of experiences, from cosmopolitan adventures to nearby woodlands and beautiful scenes by the water. Let the city’s energy sweep you off your feet and get ready for an unforgettable journey in this vibrant, urban playground.
US.SFO.destinationHighlightsH1: San Francisco: A stunning and colourful melting pot
US.SFO.eatingImageText:
Fisherman’s Wharf is where the culinary scene is quintessentially San Franciscan, with huge menus of fresh seafood. Order seafood chowder to enjoy a creamy broth packed with seafood and vegetables. The famous San Francisco sourdough that is served with chowder dates back to the Gold Rush era and it remains a staple in this city.

If you’re visiting San Francisco over a weekend, the Ferry Building Farmers Market is a must-do on a Saturday morning. It’s abundant with produce, artisanal cheeses and handcrafted delicacies showcasing the best flavours of the region.

A testament to the city’s cultural mosaic, Chinatown is a popular location for gastronomy. This bustling enclave is brimming with sizzling woks and fresh dim sum.

US.ATL.touristAttractionsText:
Discover Atlanta’s past at the Atlanta History Center and the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, which hosts guided tours of his birth home and relevant landmarks. Take a tour with the Atlanta Preservation Center to learn even more.

Sports enthusiasts will be captivated by the array of stadiums. From the Mercedes Benz Stadium – home of the Atlanta Falcons and Atlanta United FC – to baseball’s Truist Park and NASCAR’s Atlanta Motor Speedway. Visit the College Football Hall of Fame to find your team on the Helmet Wall.

For a family-friendly adventure, explore the Georgia Aquarium – one of the largest in the world. Animal lovers will also enjoy Zoo Atlanta – it’s wild fun for all ages.
US.ATL.leisureActivitiesText:
Atlanta is bursting with activities, and a great way to take in the sights is on a bike tour. Admire landmarks along the way and observe Atlanta’s Tiny Doors and street art scattered throughout the city.

Atlanta is also known for its green spaces. Wander through the Atlanta Botanical Garden and the Centennial Olympic Park. Pack a picnic, or delight in the park attractions.

Delve even deeper into Atlanta’s past at the Atlanta History Center, which presents the largest collection of Civil War memorabilia in the Southeast.

Take a day to uncover the nooks of Stone Mountain Park, renowned for its hiking, biking and jogging routes – it even boasts a golf course. At night, films are projected onto the mountain and there is a spectacular laser show.
US.ATL.shoppingText:
There are many shopping areas in Atlanta catering to different styles and budgets. In Midtown, you can browse chic boutiques with the latest fashion, accessories and home décor. It’s a great place to grab souvenirs, whether it’s an Atlanta t-shirt or local sports merchandise.

Little Five Points, Ponce City Market and Krog Street Market have a stock of eclectic and vintage pieces. Discover artisanal goods, second-hand items, and boutiques for those one-of-a-kind pieces.

Atlantic Station is bursting with brand and designer shops, while Buckhead further embraces luxury, high-end shopping. On the other end of the scale, there are numerous outlet malls in Atlanta to grab some fantastic offers.
US.ATL.destinationPageIntro: Take a flight to Atlanta to experience comforting Southern charm in a vibrant city. Discover historical landmarks, catch a sports game or indulge in diverse cuisine.
US.ATL.overviewText:
Discover a city where vibrant culture meets Southern charm. Atlanta offers a wealth of cultural experiences, from world-class museums and venues to diverse dining and a thriving arts scene. The rich history of Atlanta is woven into its contemporary evolution, with historic neighbourhoods and civil rights landmarks intertwined alongside modern attractions.

Outdoor spaces provide a welcome serenity, the perfect location for recreational activities. These parks are often filled with energy, as the city’s festival calendar is packed year-round, from music and film festivals to food and cultural celebrations showcasing the city’s lively spirit.
US.ATL.destinationHighlightsH1: Atlanta: A city of warm, Southern charm
US.ATL.eatingImageText:
Embark on a food tour to taste the history and variations of Atlanta’s cuisine.

Peachtree Roads is a hub for diverse dining, from upscale restaurants to cosy cafés. Ponce City Market is an ideal place to sample many of the city’s offerings, from artisan treats to gourmet meals.

Buckhead is popular for its fine dining and steakhouses. And, to enjoy authentic Southern fare, the Southwest area is the place to go. Order chicken and biscuits, crab cakes, and bread pudding – the best of soul food.

Atlanta is also celebrated as one of the best cities for barbecue. Whether you crave smoky ribs or fried chicken, the experience will be unforgettable.

For a truly multicultural encounter, head to Buford Highway. This international corridor boasts hundreds of bespoke eateries.

CA.YUL.touristAttractionsText:
Start your tour in Old Montreal and  admire the European grandeur of the Notre-Dame Basilica, where Gothic architecture meets an ethereal interior. Continue along the cobblestone streets where you’ll stumble upon quirky boutiques, quaint cafés and the occasional street musician.

Looking for a panoramic view of the city? Climb aboard the Le Grande Roue de Montreal, the city’s majestic Ferris wheel. As you ascend, you’ll be treated to a bird’s eye view of the sparkling cityscape below.

For a little tranquility, make your way to the green oasis of Mount Royal Park. Hike or bike along its scenic trails and visit the summit for a spectacular vista. Nearby, Saint Joseph’s Oratory of Mount Royal stands as a serene retreat with its magnificent basilica and gardens.
CA.YUL.leisureActivitiesText:
Montreal is a city that knows how to make the most of every season with unforgettable events. In the winter, the festival of Nuit Blanche transforms the city into a dazzling spectacle of glowing installations, live performances and spontaneous dance parties.

The winter adventures don’t stop there. Glide across the Old Port’s ice rink beneath a canopy of festive lights. Come summer, swap your skates for a paddle boat and float gently on the Old Port’s waters.

The Jardin botanique de Montréal is another place to explore. Come winter, it’s a snowy haven with walking trails, surrounded by trees, birds and more. It’s also perfect for cross-country skiing. Come summer, the botanical garden transforms into an enchanting lightshow for the Gardens of light festival.
CA.YUL.shoppingText:
Montreal’s bustling shopping boulevard, Rue Sainte-Catherine, is filled with high-end boutiques and contrasting bespoke stores. Each storefront is a treasure trove waiting to be explored.

A short stroll takes you to Marché Bonsecours, a two-storey indoor market that blends old-world flair with modern sophistication. Here you can find artisanal crafts, local delicacies and unique souvenirs.

Mont-Royal Avenue is another must-visit, serving as Montreal’s main shopping and dining thoroughfare. This energetic street is lined with eclectic boutiques, cafés and gourmet eateries.

For a unique adventure, explore RÉSO, Montreal’s extensive Underground City. The 32-kilometre network of tunnels and passages are home to many designer stores and an array of dining options.
CA.YUL.destinationPageIntro: Explore Canada’s French flair in Montreal, where the aroma of freshly baked bagels and café au lait sweep you off your feet and the architecture transports you back to Europe.
CA.YUL.overviewText:
Montreal is like a captivating novel, where each chapter reveals a new facet of its vibrant story. A city where French flair meets North American zest, Montreal is a unique and irresistible blend of the two. As you wander through the streets you’ll be greeted by the buzz of a city that rarely sleeps.

Sip a café au lait at a charming sidewalk café or marvel at the stunning Gothic architecture. Festivals light up the streets, street performers create wholesome moments and the culinary scene invites you to try mouthwatering classics. 

From the European charm of Old Montreal to the modern skyscrapers of Downtown, the city is like a dynamic playground of activity, ready to welcome you with open arms.
CA.YUL.eatingImageText:
Eat your way through the Marché Maisonneuve, a colourful bazaar bursting with fresh produce, artisanal cheeses and local delicacies. Smell the scent of freshly baked bread and gaze at the colours of seasonal fruits and vegetables. It’s a feast for the senses. Immerse yourself in a world of flavours at Marché Jean-Talon, an open-air market that showcases Montreal’s diverse food culture.

Your trip is not complete without a bagel in Montreal. Head to the charming neighbourhoods of Le Plateau or Mile End, where these golden rings are more than just bread – they are a tradition. Warm, slightly sweet and chewy, topped with sesame seeds, and filled with cream cheese and other inventive flavours.

Poutine, crispy fries smothered in a rich gravy and gooey cheese curds, is another must-try. You’ll love this comforting, iconic dish.

SA.DMM.touristAttractionsText:
Visit the stunning Tarout Castle, perched on its own island. This centuries-old fortress offers panoramic views, whispering tales of Dammam’s past of being a bustling trading town. Step back in time and experience traditional Saudi culture at the Heritage Village, where you can wander through old houses and savour authentic, local dishes at the village’s restaurant.

From history to the sea, the Dammam Corniche is a breath of fresh air, perfect for a sunset stroll. For a dose of creativity and innovation, visit the King Abdulaziz Centre for World Culture, a striking architectural marvel. Explore interactive exhibits that celebrate Saudi Arabia’s rich heritage and forward-thinking future.
SA.DMM.leisureActivitiesText:
Set sail on a boating or fishing excursion. Dammam’s seaside location on the Arabian Gulf makes it the perfect setting to cast a line or simply enjoy the salty breeze.

Unwind in King Fahad Park, a lush oasis where nature meets leisure. With sprawling lawns, serene lakes, and colourful flower gardens, it’s the ideal spot for a city picnic.

For family fun, head to Dolphin Island on Al Murjan Island, where you can watch mesmerising dolphin shows and other marine attractions. The island itself is a gem, with beautiful sea views and plenty to explore.

Marjan Island, also known as Coral Island, is another must-visit destination. Easily accessible from Dammam’s coastline, this island is renowned for its calm beaches, shaded picnic spots and even a zoo.
SA.DMM.shoppingText:
For a true Saudi Arabia shopping experience, head to Souq Al-Hob. Wander through the narrow alleys filled with stalls stocked with vibrant textiles, jewellery and spices. The Dammam Traditional Market is a treasure trove of local finds like handicrafts, perfumes and unique souvenirs.

Souq Al-Hob is one of the most popular shopping spots in Dammam. This pedestrian-friendly area is known as the first entrepreneurial haven for women since 1943. You’ll find all kinds of small businesses here, selling perfumes, watches, jewellery, abayas and much more.

The city is also home to many luxury malls, filled with sleek boutiques and designer brands.
SA.DMM.destinationPageIntro: The historic Tarout Castle is a must for the adults while kids will love Dolphin Village on the manmade Al-Marjan Island. Dammam also has plenty of green spaces, beaches and children's playgrounds.
SA.DMM.overviewText:
Once a quiet fishing village along the Arabian Gulf, Dammam has blossomed into a vibrant city of modernity. Take a stroll through its streets and you’ll find landmarks that pay tribute to its seafaring past, all while soaking in the energy of the contemporary hub.

Explore the age-old markets, embrace the thriving arts scene, bustle through the busy business districts, or simply relax on the lively waterfront. Whether you’re sipping coffee in a local café or wandering down its charming streets, Dammam invites you to slow down and discover its unique charm.
SA.DMM.destinationHighlightsH1: Dammam: Old-age town with a modern twist
SA.DMM.eatingImageText:
Dammam is a city of rich traditions and bold flavours, and the food is no exception. Try nejdi kabsa, a fragrant rice dish infused with spices and tender meat of lamb or chicken. The blend of cinnamon, cloves and cardamom gives it that true Saudi Arabian taste.

Dammam’s love for wood-fire cooking is evident in the deep, smoky flavours of grilled meats and flatbreads cooked in traditional ovens. Takyt Bahar is the place to go for a taste of these locally cooked dishes.

If you’re looking for something a little different, indulge in mandi, a slow-cooked feast of meat and rice from neighbouring Yemen. It’s flavoured with spices and prepared in an underground pit, giving it a distinctive flavour.

SA.TIF.touristAttractionsText:
The sweet scent of roses drifts on the breeze in Taif, as rose oil is one of its biggest exports. If you’re here in the spring you’ll see more than 300 million pink and red roses blooming in the rose plantations around the city. To buy the most authentic rose oil, visit the Al Gadhi Rose Factory, the largest in the city, and buy your rose oil straight from the source.

For a family day out, Arruddaf Park is the place to go, with dancing fountains, waterfalls, play areas for the children, and family-friendly restaurants. Or cool off at the Taif Water Park at Al Kar Tourist Village.

If you have a head for heights, hop onboard the Teleferic Taif cable car, a 20-minute trip that will take you high above the city and give you spectacular views of the mountains and surrounding countryside.
SA.TIF.leisureActivitiesText:
Taif has plenty of museums to explore, including the delightful Al Shareef Museum, which has an eclectic collection of exhibits and artefacts to explore.

 A 30-mile detour will take you out to a well-preserved Turkish Fort, with some interesting rock carvings nearby at the site of the Souk Okaz, a pre-Islamic gathering site that has significant cultural importance in this part of the region. 

Ready to get your heart pumping? If you love a bit of adventure, the Taf Zip Line will have you whizzing over the wadi at up to 55km/h in an adrenaline-fuelled ride of a lifetime.

Towering above the city are the magnificent Sarawat Mountains. A trip to the Al Shafa Village at the summit is an ideal day trip for the whole family. Remember to take a warm jumper as it can get chilly at the top!
SA.TIF.shoppingText:
As with most modern cities, Taif is a mix of chic, air-conditioned malls and busy markets. For an authentic souq experience, Al Balad Market is one of the biggest in the city and is full of perfumes, rose oil, handicrafts, jewellery and textiles, as well as fresh fruit.

For a smaller, more intimate souq, Bab Al Hazm is an old market where you can buy souvenirs and handmade items in a more relaxed, laid-back atmosphere.

The city’s malls are upscale and well stocked with outlets selling both Saudi and international brands, with plenty of food courts and entertainment options to keep everyone happy.

For a boutique shopping expedition, the winding streets of the old city are perfect for exploring, where you’ll find artisans and local tea shops side by side.
SA.TIF.destinationPageIntro: Taif is filled with gardens, historical landmarks and bustling souqs. Discover the culture, cuisine, and character of the Saudi people in this welcoming summer destination.
SA.TIF.overviewText:
In the Mecca province of Saudi Arabia is the beautiful city of Taif. This ancient settlement dates back to the 7th century, when it was a walled trading town. Sitting at the very heart of the province, Taif may be a better-suited option than Jeddah or Medinah for travellers who wish to dive deeper into the Kingdom’s rich culture after completing Hajj and Umrah. Today, it’s a popular tourist destination thanks to its cool mountain climate and spectacular scenery, as well as its diverse cultural scene.

With excellent restaurants and plenty of souqs, malls and markets to explore, Taif is a lush, green and visually stunning place that has rightfully earned its name as the ‘Summer Capital’.

The air is scented with Taif roses, used to make the world’s finest perfumes, and its succulent grapes are so good they have their own festival. Exploring Taif is a chance to delve deeper into Saudi heritage, history, and culture in exquisite surroundings.
SA.TIF.destinationHighlightsH1: Taif: The enchanting City of Roses
SA.TIF.eatingImageText:
Taif cuisine is a diverse and interesting fusion of influences. The fertile soil also makes it a key farming area, so expect to find an abundance of fruit including pomegranates and figs as well as sweet dates on offer. 

Chicken, lamb and camel meat are staples, often served with rice and cooked in rich stews such as al kabsa, a chicken or lamb dish with basmati rice and spices. 

A delicious on-the-go snack is mutabbaq, a stuffed pancake or savoury bread filled with meat or vegetables. And expect to find plenty of street vendors selling spicy sambosas.

For special occasions, expect to be served haneeth, succulent slow-cooked lamb with a unique blend of seasoning to give it a rich, full flavour. And for a sweet treat try ma’amoul, shortbread pastries filled with dates, almonds and pistachios.

SA.HAS.touristAttractionsText:
Any visit to Hail should include a trip to the magnificent Al Qishla Palace. Built in the 1940s by King Abdul Aziz, it’s an ode to the architectural brilliance of the ornamental Najdi style.

Head to A’arif Fort, an imposing structure from the 17th century that will reward you with a glimpse into the region’s past and sweeping panoramic views of the entire desert city.

Part of the Jubbah UNESCO World Heritage Site includes the astonishing 10,000-year-old cliff-face pictographs. These incredible drawings trace back to the earliest human presence in Arabia, when the desert bloomed and huge oryx roamed freely – standing as witnesses to the area’s undeniable legacy.

Stroll around AlAziziyah farm and discover a place where the grass is indeed greener. Spanning over eight million square meters, its olive groves and citrus orchards call you in for a peaceful picnic. After reconnecting with the earth, take to the air at the aviation club or trot along a camel ride.
SA.HAS.leisureActivitiesText:
Make your way to Al Nafud Desert. Its huge, crescent-shaped red dunes are perfect for high-octane 4x4 fun, and you can stay in traditional Bedouin campsites where at night, the clear desert skies are filled with stars. This adventure playground is also the perfect place to experience camel rides and safaris, quad-biking and sandboarding.

If a hike is something you can’t pass up, trek through Al Samara Park – a serene oasis with trails and magnificent views of the city from Jabal al Samra in the Shammar Mountains. At night, the lake at the centre of the park becomes the focus of attention, with sparkling lights creating an enthralling spectacle.

For more excitement-fuelled moments, join the crowds as they support the two main football teams, Al-Tai and Al-Jabalain, who compete in national and international matches at the Prince Abdulaziz bin Musaed Sports City Stadium.
SA.HAS.shoppingText:
Stroll through the Hail Souq for a traditional shopping experience. The commercial centre has been at the very heart of trade since the earliest days of the ancient desert caravans. Here, you can find hand-woven fabrics, aromatic spices, artisan rugs, silverware and gold jewellery. The atmosphere is lively, the haggling frantic and there are bargains to be had. Wander away from the main souq and you’ll also find stalls along the streets and alleyways surrounding the main square.

A little further beyond, you’ll even find plenty of modern shopping options. The city is home to several large malls offering both local goods and high-end brands, from clothing to everyday essentials. They’re a great place to shop in comfort, thanks to the cool, air-conditioned interiors.
SA.HAS.destinationPageIntro: A jewel in the Arabian Desert, Hail is packed with history, busy souqs, extraordinary landscapes and serene oases that capture the spirit of Saudi Arabia.
SA.HAS.overviewText:
Nestled in the heart of the Arabian Desert between the twin mountain ranges of Aja and Salma, Hail is a treasure that’s well worth seeking out. Surrounded by dramatic dunes and a wild, majestic expanse, this historic site played a vital role in trade along the caravan and Hajj route. It is also the birthplace of Hatim Al Tai – a famous poet and nobleman – and was renowned as a centre for learning and culture.

Today, its remarkable mud-brick heritage buildings, gorgeous oases and lush date plantations make it a tempting destination for visitors who want to step off the usual tourist trails and experience a proud and authentic Saudi city. This ‘Key to the Desert’ lives up to its name and will surpass your expectations with its warmth and fascinating culture.
SA.HAS.destinationHighlightsH1: Hail: The jewel of the Arabian Desert
SA.HAS.eatingImageText:
Hail is known for its culinary scene, blending traditional and modern flavours with panache. As an important trading hub for thousands of years, its cuisine has absorbed a wide variety of spices and influences you don’t find in other parts of the country. A staple is Hail Harees – a time-honoured dish prepared from boiled wheat grains with meat, onions and tomatoes.

Tuck into some Keubaibat – the region’s signature dish made with vine leaves stuffed with meat, vegetables and rice and served with a tomato-based sauce. For your sweet tooth, try some Hanaini dough made from dates, ghee and white bread filling – delicious way to end a meal or give yourself a calorie boost before tackling a mountain trail.

A fine blend of cultural heritage and warm ambiance, Earth Cafe invites you in for a fulfilling breakfast and traditional sip of coffee. Transformed from an ancestral home, this authentic mud house nestled within dramatic desert landscapes stands as a testament to the area’s rich history and embracing hospitality.

OM.SLL.touristAttractionsText:
Visit Al Mughsail beach, one of the most dramatic sweeps of sand in Oman. A stroll along the beach brings you to the Marneef Cave and its dramatic blowhole, where water blasts upwards at an incredible rate.

They’re at their most dramatic during the Khareef (rainy) season. If you’re visiting then, take an inland hike to Ayn Khor waterfall, with a natural pool where you can cool off with a swim in the clear water.

The history of this important trading post is documented at the Museum of the Frankincense Land, which you’ll find in the beautifully preserved Al-Baleed Archaeological Site. Along with Sumhuram Old City (Khor Rori), Wubar Archeological Site and Wadi Dawkah, these make up a fascinating UNESCO World Heritage Site and let you immerse yourself in the culture and history of the region.
OM.SLL.leisureActivitiesText:
Salalah’s festivals are famous and welcome visitors who want to learn more about the culture of this distinctive region. Watch a Dhofari Folk Dance performance, where the costumes, music and movement of the dancers tell ancient stories of Oman.

Join the locals for an afternoon of watching some camel racing. The races are thrilling, and you’ll also see demonstrations of falconry and traditional games such as Almokabasah (a type of wrestling).

Evenings bring a whole new ambience to the city, and the light and sound shows illuminating Salalah’s historic buildings are a truly spectacular experience.

Another specialty of the Salalah Festival season is the culinary explorations of the region’s food. Cooking demonstrations teach you how to cook using traditional Omani techniques and preparing spice blends.
OM.SLL.shoppingText:
Salalah has always been a hugely important trading centre, and the markets and souqs carry on this tradition. Al-Husn Souq is best for local handicrafts, especially silver jewellery and incense, Omani textiles and carvings.

Salalah Central Market is a thriving produce market where you can buy herbs, spices, and fresh ingredients.

For some air-conditioned comfort, Salalah has several malls including the new Salalah Grand Mall and the huge Salalah Gardens Mall. This expansive retail centre also offers a large food court and a children’s play area.

For some evening shopping, stroll down As Salam Street, which is lined with stores selling everything from watches and jewellery to clothes, bags and sunglasses. Nearby Ar Rubat Street also offers some busy local shops to explore.
OM.SLL.destinationPageIntro: A green oasis surrounded by majestic mountains and white sand beaches, Salalah is a year-round destination that offers fabulous food, historic sites and exciting festivals.
OM.SLL.overviewText:
Southern Oman’s capital – the country’s third largest city – is a dazzling contrast to the surrounding desert. As well as a lush, green oasis, it’s also filled with fascinating historical attractions.

Famous for the Khareef Festival as well as being the historical centre for the highly valued frankincense trade, Salalah is a charming juxtaposition of old and new, ancient and modern.

With towering mountains, crashing waterfalls and a mild climate even during the summer, Salalah is an oasis surrounded by the wild, untamed beauty of the Omani desert.

The beaches are lined with white sand, with a tempestuous sea that’s perfect for capturing dramatic photos. The markets buzz and the food is distinctive and delicious. Let Qatar Airways take you on a magical journey to Oman’s green jewel, the enchanting city of Salalah.
OM.SLL.eatingImageText:
Food in Salalah is full of flavour and draws influences from a diverse range of cultures including African, Arabic and Indian cuisine. Traditional Omani dishes include shuwa, which is melt-in-the-mouth slow-cooked lamb, and harees, a hearty wheat porridge with meat served with unleavened bread.

Other must-try dishes include madhbi, grilled meat marinated in a spicy blend and cooked over an open flame, and mishkak, which are beef or chicken kebabs cooked over a charcoal grill and served with a spicy sauce.

Head into the centre of the city and you’ll find fine dining restaurants serving a selection of cuisines, including delicious Indian food. Browse the souqs and you’ll come across vendors selling falafel and other familiar street food.

IQ.EBL.touristAttractionsText:
Nestled in the centre of Erbil, the Erbil Citadel stands proud, holding centuries of Kurdish heritage within its old walls. Stroll through its narrow lanes that date back over 6,000 years and relax in one of its famous teahouses. Surrounding the citadel are traditional homes reflecting Kurdish and Ottoman architecture, some of which have been restored and turned into cultural cafés and cultural centres.

Nearby is the Jalil Khayat Mosque, one of the largest and most beautiful mosques in the region and known for its grand architecture resembling the Blue Mosque in Istanbul.

For some fresh air, Sami Abdulrahman Park is an oasis of greenery and tranquility. Lush lawns and peaceful pathways lead you to an unexpected area filled with Italian food. Next up is Shanadar Park – a hub for local artists and musicians.
IQ.EBL.leisureActivitiesText:
Visit the enchanting Bekhal Waterfall, where water cascades down rugged cliffs into pools that seem almost otherworldly. Locals flock here for the refreshing mist on warmer days, and to experience nature at its finest.

A short drive from Erbil takes you to beautiful mountain areas such as Salahaddin or Shaqlawa – great for hiking and picnics. Korek Mountain is another standout nature spot near Erbil, especially for those looking to experience the rugged beauty of Kurdistan’s mountains.

For an experience that takes you back thousands of years, visit Shanidar Cave. It’s here that Neanderthal remains were discovered, revealing stories of early humanity. When you stand in the cool shadows of the cave, imagine the lives that unfolded here millennia ago.
IQ.EBL.shoppingText:
A must-visit for shopaholics visiting Erbil is the Qaysari Bazaar, one of the city’s oldest markets. Its maze-like alleys lead you past dazzling stalls of handmade rugs, woven with intricate patterns and colours. Each one is like a piece of art, carrying with it the spirit of the mountains and artisans who created it. It’s also worth exploring Family Mall and Majidi Mall for a modern shopping experience with plenty of cafés and entertainment options.

Look out for dried fruit pulps – chewy, sweet sheets made from apricots, plums and more. These traditional treats are beloved snacks, loaded with flavour and heritage.
IQ.EBL.destinationPageIntro: Discover Erbil, the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan. Explore some of the oldest places on Earth in a city alive with the activity of new customs and old traditions.
IQ.EBL.overviewText:
Erbil, the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan, is a city where every corner hints at stories from past empires and resilient cultures. At its heart lies a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on Earth. As you explore, you’ll find the old blending seamlessly with the new – marketplaces, contemporary cafés, and skyscrapers set against the backdrop of ancient stone walls.

It’s not just Erbil’s history that draws you in, it’s the warmth of its people. Kurdish hospitality is legendary, and here, you’re welcomed as a friend. The bazaars are filled with the sounds of laughter and chatter – one can spend hours sampling kebabs and sipping chai. Erbil offers you a glimpse into a world that feels both timeless and bursting with excitement.
IQ.EBL.eatingImageText:
The bustling Hafta Bazaar is filled with delectable spices and smoky grills. Vendors call out, offering succulent kebabs charred to perfection. Then, there’s kofta – spiced meatballs with hints of cinnamon and coriander, crispy on the outside and tender within. For a vegetarian delight, try Kurdish falafels – herb-infused chickpea patties, served with tahini and vegetables.

Another local favourite is Kurdish biryani – a fragrant masterpiece of fluffy basmati rice, topped with lamb or chicken, and mixed with warming spices like cardamom and saffron. It’s best served with yoghurt and pickles, and washed down with a cup of freshly brewed spiced chai tea.

IQ.BSR.leisureActivitiesText:
The Ahwaris or Marsh Arabs have lived in the Iraqi Marshes for centuries. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a day’s excursion takes you to meet these unique people. Travelling in a traditional mashoof (canoe), you’ll see their floating homes as well as the wildlife that inhabits the marshes.

Basra’s palm tree forests are famous, and a cool, shady place to have a leisurely picnic. You can also take a tour of the plantations to learn about their significance in the history of Basra and its importance as a trading centre.

If you’re familiar with the legend of Sinbad, a visit to the oasis of Sinbad Island is a chance to discover more about the rich maritime history of Basra. Take a stroll along the paths and green spaces, or take the kids to one of the island’s amusement arcades for some family fun.
IQ.BSR.shoppingText:
Basra has plenty of souqs and markets to explore, including the Indian Market, which is one of the city’s largest. Stalls selling everything from spices and leather goods to piles of dates, clothes and jewellery all vie for your attention. Be prepared to haggle for the best prices. Other markets to explore include the Hanna-Sheikh bazaar.

For some air-conditioned comfort and a choice of hundreds of stores, a trip to Basra’s newest mall is a must. This huge new structure brings together both local sellers and international brands, as well as offering entertainment and a large food court.

Take a walk down Al-Gazar Street and you’ll come to more mall shopping options as well as busy stores and shops with plenty of retail experiences for the dedicated shopper.
IQ.BSR.destinationPageIntro: Basra is a crossroads where ancient and modern cultures meet, creating a unique and fascinating city break destination. This culturally rich location is a traveller’s delight.
IQ.BSR.overviewText:
Iraq’s third-largest city sits close to the border with Iran and Kuwait, making this ancient trading post a cosmopolitan and lively city. Once known as the ‘Venice of the East’ because of the number of canals and waterways, it sits at the heart of one of the most fertile and lush locations in Iraq.

From forests of date palms to busy markets, traditional dhow river tours and kayaking adventures, there’s plenty to see and do in this jewel of a city. Discover its ancient history in Old Basra, or try authentic Iraqi food in its many restaurants.

Haggle for bargains in the souqs, or take a day trip to see the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Iraqi Marshes, home to one of the oldest communities of Marsh Arabs. Basra is a revelation just waiting to be discovered by adventurous travellers.
IQ.BSR.touristAttractionsText:
The heart of the city is the mighty Shatt al-Arab river where the Tigris and the Euphrates rivers meet. Get a different perspective on Basra with a tour down the river, taking you past the city on a traditional dhow boat.

The history of Basra stretches back eons and you can see some of the most important artefacts and learn more with a visit to the Basra Museum.

For a kayaking trip with a difference, hire a kayak and paddle down the Ashar Creek that cuts right through the middle of the city. It’s a unique way to see the old and new architecture that lines this waterway.

The Corniche al-Basra has been fully renovated and is now a charming place to take an evening walk along the nature promenade, where you’re surrounded by beautifully manicured gardens and art installations.
IQ.BSR.destinationHighlightsH1: Basra: Iraq’s jewel on the Shatt al-Arab
IQ.BSR.eatingImageText:
Basrawi cuisine draws its influences from Persia, the Middle East, and India. A favourite dish is masgouf, which is grilled fish (often carp) that’s slow-cooked on an open fire. Masgouf is the Iraqi national dish and is cooked using olive oil, rock salt, tamarind, and ground turmeric.

Another popular dish is qoozi, which is lamb stuffed with rice, nuts, and raisins and slow roasted. For on-the-go food, falafels and dolma (vine leaves stuffed with rice and meat or vegetables) are sold on every street corner. Or try kubba halab, a snack made from ground beef or lamb mixed with rice and spices and then fried or baked and served with yoghurt and cucumber salad.

For a sweet treat try geymar, water buffalo cream served with dates, sesame seeds and drizzled with honey.

IR.MHD.touristAttractionsText:
The Imam Reza Shrine Complex is the most important destination in Mashhad and Iran’s holiest site. This mausoleum belongs to the eight Iman of Shia Islam and is truly a magnificent complex that includes a huge library and the exquisite Goharshad Mosque, one of the largest mosques in the world.

The city embraces the arts, and you’ll find plenty of beautiful sculptures dotted around the parks and streets. Take a guided tour to find out more about the artists involved. There are also museums and galleries to explore.

For younger explorers, Water Waves Land is a family day out with slides, pools and plenty of fun for all ages. Or spend the day scrambling over the miniature mountain in the middle of the delightful Koohsangi Park, which also has a large lake and some very good ice cream stalls.
IR.MHD.leisureActivitiesText:
For a quiet escape from the hustle and bustle of the streets, Mellat Park is a haven of tranquillity, with a small amusement park that offers plenty of rides and attractions. During the evening, the park’s musical fountain puts on a beautiful light and sound display.

Take a day trip to the nearby city of Tus, one of the most important centres for Persian poetry and home of the poet Ferdowsi, author of the Book of Kings. His life and works are celebrated at the Tomb of Ferdowsi.

One of the region’s unique attractions, Kang Village, is around an hour by car but affords an incredible glimpse into traditional rural Iranian life. This pretty village clambers up steep slopes and has distinctive architecture, narrow alleyways and friendly locals. Kang Village is also a starting point for many hiking paths that criss-cross the area.
IR.MHD.shoppingText:
Mashhad is a great shopping destination. It has three large bazaars, Bazaar Reza, Kuwaiti Bazaar and Bazaar-e bozorg-e Makazy. Things to look out for when you’re treasure hunting include authentic Khorasan crafts and jewellery, Oud perfumes and the most famous of Iranian products, saffron.

The best neighbourhoods for shopping include Sajjad Blvd with its luxury boutiques and designer stores. Daneshgah Ave is known for shops selling leather bags and travel goods, while Rahnamayi is the best street to buy clothing and gold.

For traditional Persian carpets, the Carpet Bazaar near the shrine is filled with artisan stores selling genuine Persian rugs in all sizes and designs. If you prefer a more modern shopping experience, the city has several large, air-conditioned malls.
IR.MHD.destinationPageIntro: Iran’s holiest city is a beautiful mix of ancient spirituality and culture with a modern heart. Mashhad is vibrant and welcoming all year round.
IR.MHD.overviewText:
Situated in northeastern Iran, close to Turkmenistan and Afghanistan, Mashhad is a jewel that attracts visitors from around the world. As Iran’s second-largest population centre, Mashhad is considered the holiest city and spiritual heart of the country, with the dazzling Imam Reza Holy Shrine at its centre.

It’s also a family-friendly destination, with lush open spaces and water parks for younger visitors. Food lovers will enjoy experiencing the unique cuisine of northern Iran, inspired by a variety of different cultures and packed with flavour.

Thanks to its cooler temperatures, Mashhad is ideal to visit all year round. Alongside its ancient cultural importance is a thriving, modern metropolis with air-conditioned malls, an excellent travel network, and plenty to see and do.
IR.MHD.destinationHighlightsH1: Mashhad: The spiritual heart of Iran
IR.MHD.eatingImageText:
Mashhad’s food culture is a key part of its identity, with local dishes such as Sholeh Mashhadi, regarded as a heritage dish in Iran. This rich stew is a staple food in the city, along with others like Dizi Sangi, a potato, bean and lamb stew or Shishlik Shandiz, which are lamb chops in saffron.

Desserts like Changali are a delicious afternoon snack, made from fried bread covered in honey. For a cool treat, the city has many shops selling Persian ice cream in flavours like peach, vanilla and coffee. Street food is plentiful, like hot and tasty kebabs and filled pita breads.

Restaurants offer fusion cuisine from traditional French fare to authentic Iranian and Persian delights. Persian dishes tend to focus more on flavour rather than spice, usually comprised of thick stews served with flatbread and fragrant rice.

IR.SYZ.touristAttractionsText:
A visit to Hafez’s Tomb is a must when you visit Shiraz. Regarded as one of the greatest Persian poets, Hafez’s Tomb is a beautiful mausoleum surrounded by immaculately maintained gardens filled with references to Hafez’s poetry. Shiraz is home to a wealth of poets, and other cultural locations include the tomb of master poet Sa’di.

As well as literary wonders, Shiraz is famous for its gardens, including Eram Garden, a complex of enchanting gardens linked by an intricate canal system and filled with delicate flowers.

Dominating the downtown area is the citadel of the Arg of Karim Khan, with towering sandstone walls surrounding a beautiful garden and buildings. The Qur’an Gate, the city’s main gate, is also well worth a visit and is one of the finest architectural designs in Iran.
IR.SYZ.leisureActivitiesText:
Just 35 minutes away from the centre of Shiraz is the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Persepolis, which is an essential day trip for any visitor to the city. This ancient metropolis is truly magnificent, despite being razed to the ground by Alexander the Great and is filled with fabulous photo opportunities.

For a truly special place to capture a rainbow of colours, the Nasir-ol-Molk Mosque is the place to go. Also known as the Pink Mosque or the Rainbow Mosque, it’s a photographer’s dream, especially early in the morning as the light illuminates the mosque’s colourful windows.

Just over 20 miles from downtown Shiraz is Ghalat Village, where you can see traditional clay and stone houses, and eat traditional Persian food. The village gives visitors a glimpse into life in a bygone era.
IR.SYZ.shoppingText:
Bazaar Vakil isn’t just a market, it’s an experience. This ancient souq is where you’ll find authentic Persian rugs, textiles, handicrafts and stalls selling precious spices like saffron. Expect to haggle, and pick up a bag of dates to munch as you browse the stalls.

Part of the Bazaar is Saraye Moshir, the best place to find the best artisan handicrafts in the region. And make sure you include a visit to Haji Bazaar, the oldest and most historic souq in Shiraz.

Shiraz has some excellent shopping malls that offer air-conditioned comfort and retail outlets, food halls and entertainment. Aftab Fars Shopping Centre is one of the biggest, or spend an afternoon exploring the Persian Gulf Complex, one of the largest malls in the world and home to an amusement park as well as a large food court.
IR.SYZ.destinationPageIntro: With restaurants on every corner and so much history on display, Shiraz is a cultural destination with a warm, vibrant nature. It will enchant you from the moment you arrive.
IR.SYZ.overviewText:
Nestling in the south of Iran is the jewel that is Shiraz. This Persian centre of poetry and culture was once the capital of Iran, and today is the central city of Fars Province. The cosmopolitan makeup of its population makes it an eclectic and relaxed destination where everyone is welcome.

Take a wander around the well-preserved citadel of the Arg of Karim Khan, or adjourn to the air-conditioned cool of one of the city’s large shopping malls, where retail opportunities sit alongside excellent dining experiences.

Beyond the city limits are some of Iran’s most spectacular UNESCO World Heritage Sites, making Shiraz a fabulous base for discovering the culture and ancient history of Persia. The best time to visit Shiraz is spring, when the sweet scent of the orange trees hangs fills the air.
IR.SYZ.destinationHighlightsH1: Shiraz: Iran’s city of poetry and art
IR.SYZ.eatingImageText:
Iranian food is full of flavour and includes everything from light street food to hearty stews and rice dishes.

A dish found only in the city is Kalam Polo, made from meatballs, chopped cabbage and rice with a unique blend of herbs and spices. Main courses usually come with a Shirazi salad made from cucumbers, tomatoes, onions, and a simple lemon dressing.

If you’re an early riser, try a soup made from vegetables and meat called Ashe Sabzi Shirazi that’s only served from 5 to 7 am.

A delicious on-the-go snack is Shirini Nokhodchi or chickpea cookies, or look out for freshly made halva. If you have a sweet tooth, try faloodeh, an ice cream made from rice starch with different flavoured sugar waters. It’s a refreshing palate cleanser after a kebab with rice or a mutton stew.

BE.BRU.touristAttractionsText:
Begin your sightseeing at the renowned Grand-Place – often hailed as the most beautiful square in the world. The stunning Gothic and Baroque buildings create a backdrop that looks like it’s straight out of a fairytale. While you’re there, don’t miss the Mannekin-Pis, a small but iconic statue that’s become a symbol of the city.  

Next up, hop on a quick tram ride to the Atomium. This unique structure is a nod to innovation and futuristic design. You can even go inside and climb up for panoramic views of the city. 

For a dose of contemporary culture, head to Bozar. This dynamic cultural centre, housed in a striking architectural masterpiece, is a hub for all things art. Whether you’re into exhibitions, concerts, or film screenings, there’s always something happening here. And as you explore Brussels, keep an eye out for the comic strip murals splashed across walls throughout the city.
BE.BRU.leisureActivitiesText:
Venture to Bois de la Cambre, a verdant park where nature takes centre stage. It’s the perfect spot for picnics, a fun bike ride or even a boat trip to the little island café inside. 

For a deep dive into Brussels’ rich history, make your way to the Museum of the City of Brussels. Here, you’ll explore the city’s fascinating past through a collection of tapestries, sculptures and artworks.

And get this – in Brussels, you can see all of Europe in one go. Head to Mini-Europe, where all the continent’s major landmarks are recreated in miniature. It’s a fun and whimsical way to explore Europe’s highlights. 

Visiting in winter? Brussels transforms into a wonderland with its festive markets filling the air with the scent of hot waffles and holiday cheer.
BE.BRU.shoppingText:
First stop, Rue Neuve – Brussels’ answer to Oxford Street or Fifth Avenue. This bustling pedestrian street is a hub for fashion enthusiasts, lined with all the brands and high-end shops you know and love.

For a touch of grandeur, browse the architectural wonder of Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert. Its three arcades are flooded with natural light, and house everything from luxury boutiques, to artisanal chocolatiers, old-school bookshops and more.

Treasure hunters, get ready to rummage through the Jeu de Balle flea market. This open-air extravaganza is overflowing with vintage artwork, retro furniture, and one-of-a-kind antiques. You never know what hidden gems you might find.

Looking for something authentic to take back home? Pick up some exquisite Belgian lace. These delicate, handwoven pieces make the most beautiful souvenirs. Plus, it’s a true testament to the incredible craftmanship Brussels is famous for.
BE.BRU.destinationPageIntro: From the divinity of Grand-Place, to the impressive architecture on almost every corner, you won’t be short of things to marvel at in Brussels.
BE.BRU.overviewText:
Brussels is calling, and it’s bringing all its charm. This city is steeped in history, with a vibrant European vibe that’s hard to resist. Prepare to be wowed by the Art Nouveau architecture – it’s a feast for the eyes. The legacy of design visionaries like Henry van de Velde and Victor Horta lives on in the buildings, with their elaborate ironwork balconies and ornate stained-glass windows. 

Tucked away on charming, leafy streets, you’ll stumble upon art galleries, fascinating museums and quirky boutiques. Lively markets burst with unique treasures and the pavement cafés spill over with laughter and chatter – the perfect soundtrack to your stroll. 

Whether you’re relaxing in a lush park, treating yourself to a truly authentic Belgian waffle, or simply marvelling at the stunning town square, Brussels will capture your heart.
BE.BRU.eatingImageText:
When it comes to food, Brussels is a feast for the senses. The Chasseurs Ardennais Market is the place to go to taste all the incredible flavours of the region. Think fresh fruits and veggies, artisanal cheeses and delicious deli delights. Plus, there are food trucks serving tasty treats. 

Wolf is another must-see – it’s a huge street food market housed in a former bank. You’ll find a variety of international options here – from fresh sushi to classic Belgian dishes and everything in between.

Looking for something hearty and delicious? Tuck into a pot of moules frites – a giant pot of fresh mussels served with crispy fries.

A trip to Brussels isn’t complete without a proper Belgian waffle – warm, golden and dusted with powdered sugar. Pair one with a steaming coffee, and you’ve basically captured the essence of Belgian happiness. And naturally, when in Belgium, you must treat yourself to the delight of Belgian chocolate – it’s iconic for a reason!

HU.BUD.touristAttractionsText:
Take a scenic ride on the Funicular up to Buda Castle, with panoramic views of the city and the sparkling Danube. Inside, the Hungarian National Gallery exhibits centuries of art, while the Budapest History Museum provides a glimpse into the city’s past. The Széchényi National Library, home of Hungary’s literary heritage, is also based there.

After exploring Buda, meander through Pest and admire an open-air display of murals across several buildings. From here, head to Fisherman’s Bastion, a fairytale-like terrace with towers that seem to hail from another era.

Down by the river, the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial is a poignant tribute to the lives lost in World War II. For an uplifting mix of neoclassical architecture, end off your sightseeing at the majestic St Stephen’s Basilica.
HU.BUD.leisureActivitiesText:
For a true taste of Budapest, dip into the Széchenyi Baths to relax your mind and body. The thermal waters and grand architecture of the place make for a delightful escape, whether it’s in winter or summer.

Once you’re feeling refreshed, drift between Buda and Pest during a boat ride on the Danube and marvel at the city from the water. Then trek over to Margaret Island, an oasis in the Danube, where quiet trails, dancing fountains and gardens create a peaceful retreat.

If you’re looking for a family activity, make your way to the Children’s Railway, a narrow-gauge train running through Buda Hills. It’s operated almost entirely by children – except the driver of course. To experience another mode of transport, hop on one of Budapest’s iconic yellow trams and take in the city’s sights.
HU.BUD.shoppingText:
Shopping in Budapest is like a treasure hunt, where every find tells a story of Hungary’s past and present. Ecseri Market, the largest flea market in the city, is brimming with vintage finds and hidden gems. Stumble upon old Soviet memorabilia, handmade lace or timeworn records.

For those with an eye for art and curios, Falk Miksa Street is a dream come true. Known as Budapest’s antique row, it’s lined with galleries and shops presenting Hungarian paintings, sculptures and rare books.

Bring a taste of Budapest home with locally produced paprika, a staple of Hungarian cuisine. Or shop for porcelain and Ajka crystal, a piece of Hungary’s renowned craftmanship to cherish as a keepsake.
HU.BUD.destinationPageIntro: Explore two sides of Budapest in Buda and Pest. From the quaint and ancient architecture, to the fun, family-friendly activities, there’s plenty to enjoy.
HU.BUD.overviewText:
Step into a tale of two worlds in Budapest, as the city is divided by the mighty Danube. One side, Buda, rests atop a hill crowned by ancient castles and cobbled lanes. The other, Pest, buzzes with energy and thrives with art, music and contemporary vibrancy.

The thermal baths are the heartbeat of Budapest, where the art of relaxation has been perfected over the centuries. Look up, and the skyline dazzles while charming trams trundle along, offering picture-perfect views to its riders. It’s a city where there’s something to discover on every corner – a mural, a ruin or a statue with a story.

Whether you’re drawn to its grandeur or its quirks, Budapest will undoubtedly charm you throughout your journey.
HU.BUD.destinationHighlightsH1: Budapest: A timeless city on the Danube
HU.BUD.eatingImageText:
A trip to Budapest isn’t complete without trying a steaming bowl of goulash. This robust beef stew, rich in paprika, vegetables and tender meat, embodies the warmth of Hungarian kitchens. After a hearty meal, stop by the Hold Utca Food Market for a showcase of local ingredients. Overflowing with fresh produce, meats and artisanal foods, it’s a feast for the senses.

Grab what you need to whip up a tempting dish, before diving into the culinary excellence of the Great Market Hall. As soon as you walk in, you’ll be welcomed by the scent of lángos, a crispy fried dough topped with sour cream and cheese. It’s a must-try street food snack. For a sweet finish, indulge in kürtőskalács, a chimney cake. Rolled in cinnamon sugar and baked to perfection, this dessert captures the essence of Budapest.

RO.OTP.touristAttractionsText:
Kick off your adventure at the Romanian Athenaeum, a stunning neoclassical concert hall famed for its domed ceiling and intricate frescoes. Often hailed as the “temple of music”, it hosts a variety of performances year-round.

Just a short walk away, you’ll discover the Cesianu-Racovita Palace, a hidden gem with Art Nouveau flair. Once a gathering place for Romania’s elite, its rooms are filled with stories from Bucharest’s rich past.

Nearby, the Arch of Triumph stands as a proud symbol of the city’s resilience. Climb to the top for breathtaking views of Bucharest. Not far from here, the Stavropoleos Monastery offers a tranquil retreat amid the city’s liveliness, featuring bespoke wooden carvings and a serene courtyard.

Be sure to experience the grandeur of the Palace of Parliament, an immense structure and one of the largest buildings in the world.
RO.OTP.leisureActivitiesText:
The Grigore Antipa National Museum of Natural History is a treasure trove for curious minds and biodiversity enthusiasts. With immersive exhibits ranging from towering dinosaur skeletons to sparkling mineral displays, it has been a beacon of discovery for over a century.

For a quieter yet equally fascinating stop, visit the Zambaccian Museum, a memorial house turned gallery. Wander through its rooms and uncover Romanian artworks collected by Krikor Zambaccian – each piece with its own captivating story.

Step into Old Town, where cobbled streets and charming facades lead you to cosy cafés and intriguing shops. It’s the perfect spot for leisurely strolls. Need a breath of fresh air? Head to Cismigiu Gardens – an enchanting park with winding walkways, vibrant flowerbeds and rowboats gliding over tranquil lakes.
RO.OTP.shoppingText:
Start your shopping journey at Calea Victoriei, Bucharest’s grandest shopping boulevard, where luxury boutiques sit alongside quaint shops. This historic street is lined with elegant storefronts that beckon with handmade jewellery, high-end fashion and unique Romanian designer pieces.

For a more traditional experience, head to Strada Valea Cascadelor Market – a vibrant scene of colourful stalls offering wool clothing with detailed patterns unique to Romania’s rural communities.

Don’t miss the beautiful Horezu ceramics, renowned for their hand-painted motifs in earthy greens, blues, and reds. These exquisite ceramics are not just pottery, but pieces of art, capturing the heart of Romanian folk traditions.
RO.OTP.destinationPageIntro: Venture to Bucharest, the capital of Romania and stand in awe of the stunning architecture that spans centuries of history.
RO.OTP.overviewText:
Bucharest, the capital of Romania, is affectionately known as the ‘Little Paris of the East’ due to its stunning architecture. The city, once brimming with Belle Époque buildings, still showcases these gems amidst a blend of grand palaces, Soviet-era buildings, and modern skyscrapers. 

Stroll down the city’s renowned shopping streets, where chic boutiques with art deco facades and bustling cafés capture the bohemian soul of Bucharest. Or venture into Old Town’s winding streets, where historical landmarks and bistros offer an inviting blend of old-world charm.

Bucharest’s energy is infectious, its people are warm, and its spirit is undeniable. From charming tea houses to the thriving arts scene, the city enchants you with every step.
RO.OTP.destinationHighlightsH1: Bucharest: Little Paris of the East
RO.OTP.eatingImageText:
Eat your way around Piața Obor Market, where you’ll find fresh produce from the mountains, honey and vendors selling homemade cheeses. It’s a lively snapshot of Romania’s heartland right in the city.

Venture into Lipscani, the heart of Old Town, and explore the local tea houses and restaurants. Sip on a fragrant brew or savour some sarmale – tender cabbage rolls filled with spiced minced meat and paired with creamy polenta.

For a culinary adventure, try ciorbă de burtă, or tripe soup – a hearty, creamy dish that’s seasoned with vinegar and garlic. Another must-try is Romanian borsch – a sour soup made from fermented wheat bran. It comes in many variations but is always delicious.

BG.SOF.touristAttractionsText:
You can explore much of Sofia’s charming city centre on foot. A guided walking tour takes you around landmarks such as the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral and the ancient Roman Serdika complex. But it also takes you down cobbled streets and into the older sections of the city.

If you get thirsty along the way, don’t worry. Sofia is full of mineral springs, and you can fill up your water bottle for free at the city’s public bath.

When you’re at Serdika metro station you’ll find a hidden gem next to the recently uncovered Roman remains. For an unusual view of Largo Square above, there’s a ‘secret’ entrance to a lower-level viewing point with a glass roof.

If you plan a visit to Sofia as a city break destination in the winter, you’re just a short distance from some of the best skiing in Europe on uncrowded slopes.
BG.SOF.leisureActivitiesText:
Sofia has a rich cultural and arts scene to dive into. A visit to the Ivan Vazov National Theatre or the National Palace of Culture concert hall at the end of Vitosha Boulevard is highly recommended. To see Sofia’s more recent artistic endeavours, take a free tour of its unique graffiti and vivid city murals.

Sofia is famous for its beautiful architecture, but don’t miss the Banya Bashi Mosque, designed by Mimar Sinan in the 16th century. It’s a tranquil, serene place built in the Ottoman style.

Sofia has some beautiful open spaces, including City Garden in front of the National Theatre, the peace of Borisova Garden, and the family-friendly South Park. Discover the natural splendour of the region with hiking tours that take you up Mount Vitosha for exquisite views of the city below.
BG.SOF.shoppingText:
From street markets to modern malls, there’s lots of choice for retail lovers in Sofia. The Women’s Market is the oldest market in the city, selling everything from fruit and vegetables to traditional clothing, artisan crafts, spices and souvenirs.

The Central Covered Market is next to Serdika metro station and is a fun place to browse for bargains. For leisurely shopping, Vitosha Boulevard is full of brands and boutiques and is pedestrianised so it’s a relaxing place to wander. If you want a slightly quirky street experience, head to Shishman Street for art galleries, or Pirotska Street for a glimpse of Old Sofia.

For mall shopping, Paradise Center is the largest mall in the city, while Serdika Center and Park Center are more relaxed and family-friendly shopping experiences.
BG.SOF.destinationPageIntro: Explore the natural beauty of Mount Vitosha, hunt for curios in Bitaka, or admire Byzantine architecture in the city centre. Welcome to Sofia - the heart and soul of Bulgaria.
BG.SOF.overviewText:
A treasure trove of ancient architecture, fascinating museums and fine dining, Bulgaria’s capital is one of those hidden Baltic gems that’s definitely worth exploring. Nestled beneath the towering Mount Vitosha, it’s filled with Ottoman sites of cultural significance, Roman remains, and exclusive galleries.

A juxtaposition of old and new, Sofia is a family destination too, with plenty of activities for younger adventurers. Gastronomes will adore the exquisite food, with a cluster of Michelin-starred restaurants on offer.

While the city may be small in comparison to other European destinations, Sofia has plenty to offer outdoors lovers, culture seekers, and curious travellers. City break destinations don’t get much better than this charming capital surrounded by some of Bulgaria’s most beautiful countryside.
BG.SOF.eatingImageText:
Sofia is a food-lover’s paradise. With 20 or so Michelin-star restaurants clustered around the centre, you have a huge choice of fine dining. For a more authentic Bulgarian experience, look out for klek shops, open for snacks and drinks late into the evening. You’ll have to look down for these, as klek means ‘squat’ – these shops are at basement level!

Sofia’s markets are full of delicious treats including the many cheeses that are so popular in this part of the world. For breakfast, drop into one of the city’s many coffee shops and order a ‘princess’, a sandwich filled with minced meat and cheese.

Or try banitsa for breakfast, a delicious combination of whisked eggs, Bulgarian yoghurt and crumbled white cheese baked in filo pastry. And don’t leave Sofia without trying some authentic moussaka.

TN.TUN.touristAttractionsText:
Explore the majestic 8th-century wonder, Ez-Zitouna Mosque, located in the heart of the Medina. You can’t miss it rising above the city’s narrow streets. Close by is Dar Lasram, an opulent 18th-century gem. Stroll through its grand halls feeling rather royal, as it was once home to Tunisian aristocracy and has now become a cultural beacon.

Make your way to Kasbah Square, where revolution once sparked – a square brimming with history and political energy. Take a walk to Ville Nouvelle (Tunis New Town), to experience its charming mix of colonial French architecture and cosmopolitan cafés. If you have some time to spare, let the brutalist beauty of Hotel du Lac inspire you – its unique, tiered design is a symbol of post-independence innovation.
TN.TUN.leisureActivitiesText:
Venture to the National Bardo Museum, home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. Wander through its ornate halls and admire these magnificent works. For some peace, tranquility and perhaps a picnic, explore the green space at Belvedere Park. 

Craving the sun and the sea instead? La Marsa Beach is the place to be to soak up the Mediterranean atmosphere. Tuck into some freshly caught seafood at nearby coastal cafés while you’re there.

Step back in time at Carthage, where the ruins of the largest Roman baths outside Rome proudly stand. For an even deeper dive into Tunisian history, take a day trip to Dougga. This UNESCO-listed treasure trove of Roman ruins is nestled in the rolling hills. Explore its marvelous ancient theatre and temple ruins for a day of adventure.
TN.TUN.shoppingText:
Explore the majestic 8th-century wonder, Ez-Zitouna Mosque, located in the heart of the Medina. You can’t miss it rising above the city’s narrow streets. Close by is Dar Lasram, an opulent 18th-century gem. Stroll through its grand halls feeling rather royal, as it was once home to Tunisian aristocracy and has now become a cultural beacon.

Take a walk to Ville Nouvelle (Tunis New Town), to experience its charming mix of colonial French architecture and cosmopolitan cafés. If you have some time to spare, let the brutalist beauty of Hotel du Lac inspire you – its unique, tiered design is a symbol of post-independence innovation.
TN.TUN.destinationPageIntro: Tunis beckons – explore its cultural hotspots including the Medina, 8th-century Ez-Zitouna Mosque and unique architecture of the now abandoned, Hotel du Lac.
TN.TUN.overviewText:
Tunis, the charming capital of Tunisia, is steeped in history and culture, capturing the relaxed energy of the Mediterranean. Discover tales of ancient Tunisian civilisations while catching a glimpse of modern life in its innovative streets. 

Life in Tunis moves at its own pace. Start your mornings with fresh pastries and strong coffee, while afternoons are spent losing yourself in the maze-like alleys in the Medina.

Immerse yourself in the unique rhythm of Tunis, with its cultural blends of Arab and Berber influences, sea breezes sweeping through the streets, and the rich aroma of Tunisian delicacies cooking away in street stalls. Every turn in Tunis brings something unexpected and unforgettable.
TN.TUN.destinationHighlightsH1: Tunis: A marvel by the Mediterranean Sea
TN.TUN.eatingImageText:
Venture to the National Bardo Museum, home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. Wander through its ornate halls and admire these magnificent works. For some peace, tranquility and perhaps a picnic, explore the green space at Belvedere Park.
